title: Giant Iceberg Survives a Head-On Collision with an Island
summary:
In August 2026, a colossal iceberg—about the size of St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands—broke away from Petermann Glacier on Greenland's northwest coast. It was the largest calving event (when a chunk of glacier breaks off) from any Arctic glacier since 2020. But the drama didn't end there. After drifting down Petermann Fjord, the ice island collided with a small rocky outcrop called Joe Island. And remarkably, it survived the impact intact.

"We were certainly watching closely as it interacted with Joe Island and were impressed that it survived the interaction without further fragmentation," said Adam Garbo, a doctoral student at the University of Ottawa who first spotted the calving using satellite imagery. This is surprising because Petermann's icebergs are generally thinner and more fragile than those from glaciers like Jakobshavn and Helheim. In 2010, a similar ice island struck Joe Island and split in two.

The new ice island measured just over 76 square kilometers (29 square miles) when it broke off. Scientists had actually been anticipating an even larger break—they were monitoring several major rifts that seemed likely to cut across the entire ice tongue. Instead, the glacier fractured along a different crack, producing a smaller island than expected. As of late August, two large rifts remain, and researchers expect them to release new ice islands of roughly 94 and 84 square kilometers, though no one knows when.

Iceberg calving is a normal part of glacier life, but scientists monitor these events closely for signs of instability. Petermann is one of Greenland's largest marine-terminating glaciers and helps control the flow of ice from the Greenland Ice Sheet into the ocean. Changes in its stability could have implications for sea level rise.

After the collision, winds and currents carried the iceberg out of the fjord, and satellite images show it pivoting away from Joe Island and moving southwest through Nares Strait. Its journey will become more destructive over time—tides, winds, currents, and melting will weaken it until it eventually fractures. Some thicker icebergs may scrape along the seabed or become grounded, and many Petermann ice islands eventually ground near Coburg and Baffin islands.

Glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College has been tracking the iceberg using Landsat imagery. The collision was captured by Landsat 9 on August 23 and 24. This event highlights the dynamic nature of Greenland's glaciers and the importance of monitoring them as the climate changes. What will happen to this resilient iceberg next? Scientists will be watching.
why_it_matters: Greenland's glaciers are one of the biggest potential contributors to sea-level rise, so calving events in the Arctic are more than distant curiosities. For today's teens, how fast and how often glaciers shed ice will shape coastal flooding, climate policy, and the future of communities living near the world's oceans.

background_read: Greenland is covered by the Greenland Ice Sheet, a vast layer of ice that in places is over a mile thick.
Ice does not stay still: it oozes toward the coast through outlet glaciers, and Petermann Glacier is one of the largest outlet glaciers in northwest Greenland.
The front of Petermann floats as an ice tongue, and when pieces snap off, they become giant tabular icebergs, often called ice islands.
Petermann lost a massive ice island in 2010 that collided with Joe Island, a small rocky outcrop in Petermann Fjord, and broke apart; that makes the 2026 collision described here surprising.
Such remote events are watched using satellites such as Landsat 9, an Earth-observation mission run jointly by NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey.

perspectives.description: The iceberg's survival gave scientists an unplanned natural experiment, showing how a large ice island can collide with an island without immediately breaking. These observations improve computer models of iceberg movement and glacier behavior.

While one calving event is natural, repeated large calvings from Petermann may be a sign of glacier instability in a warming Arctic. If this pattern becomes more common, the Greenland Ice Sheet could lose ice faster, pushing sea levels higher and affecting millions of people.

A single iceberg collision does not by itself prove climate change is accelerating. Scientists need long records to compare the frequency and size of calving events over decades and tell whether the glacier's behavior is truly changing.

The remaining rifts on Petermann could release new ice islands, and their future paths will determine whether they endanger shipping or become grounded in Arctic waters. Continued satellite monitoring will be essential as the climate warms and Greenland's glaciers respond.
